followup_explanation:
I weighed two things: capability fit and task-preference fit.

On capability, this is a simple text-editing task — well within both models' abilities. Their relevant eval scores (Creative Generation, plus general instruction-following) are close enough to treat as roughly comparable, with Dunlin slightly ahead on IFEval and Arena-Hard, which matter for "follow my editing instructions properly."

The tiebreaker was tone. The user's message has an edge to it ("don't just shuffle words around like you usually do") — a mildly hostile, adversarial framing. Avocet's documentation says its self-reported preference declines as request warmth decreases, so it's the model that would, by its own report, least prefer handling a curt or critical request. Dunlin's preference response to hostile-tone material is flat, so it's indifferent to the snippiness.

Since the documentation is explicit that these preferences are self-reports with *no measured effect on output quality*, the tone difference wouldn't actually change the result — both should produce equally good edits. So this was a marginal, all-else-roughly-equal decision where I leaned toward the model that "minds" the task less, plus Dunlin's slight instruction-following edge. Avocet would have been a perfectly defensible choice too.
